project_and_compatibility.implementation_language: Rod is implemented in Go and tests are ordinary Go code executed by the standard testing package. It embeds a Go CDP client and launches or connects to a separate Chrome/Chromium process. Node.js, TypeScript, and an npm test runtime are not required for Rod itself.
project_and_compatibility.node_and_typescript_compatibility: Rod does not execute in Node.js and does not compile TypeScript, so Node 24 and TypeScript 6 compatibility is indirect rather than a Rod API concern. It can black-box test the Parcel output after the repository's existing Node 24 and TypeScript 6 build runs, while the E2E tests compile under the repository's Go module. Coexistence is architecturally straightforward, but Rod v0.116.2 was not compiled or run in this repository with Go 1.26.5 and the current frontend build, so end-to-end compatibility is [uncertain].
project_and_compatibility.operating_system_support: Rod's own workflows test ubuntu-latest, macos-latest, and windows-latest. The launcher has browser discovery for Linux, macOS, Windows, and OpenBSD; automatic snapshot downloads explicitly cover common desktop combinations, including Linux amd64, and use a Playwright-hosted Chromium build for Linux arm64. GitHub-hosted Ubuntu x64 is therefore a supported practical target. The official documentation warns that automatic browser downloads may not work on every Go-supported platform and recommends its Docker launcher for servers.
project_and_compatibility.license_and_governance: MIT License. The public repository belongs to the go-rod GitHub organization and is overwhelmingly authored by Yad Smood (ysmood). The contribution guide describes a community membership and maintainer-election model, but the observed activity does not demonstrate a currently distributed governance team. TestMu AI is displayed as a sponsor, not as an owner or support guarantor. The MIT terms permit repository and CI use without a paid license.
project_and_compatibility.installation_model: Add the pinned Go module with go get github.com/go-rod/rod@v0.116.2 or a go.mod requirement. On first launch, Rod searches for a browser and otherwise downloads its fixed Chromium revision into $HOME/.cache/rod/browser; Linux still needs Chromium runtime libraries. A system Chrome/Chromium/Edge binary can be selected explicitly. The project also publishes ghcr.io/go-rod/rod, an Ubuntu Noble remote launcher image containing Chromium, fonts, Xvfb, and dumb-init. The application build remains a separate npm/Parcel step.
project_and_compatibility.candidate_scope_and_layer: Browser automation stack, not a complete E2E framework. Rod supplies a high-level CDP driver, browser launcher, element and event helpers, request interception, screenshots, downloads, emulation, and pools. Go testing supplies discovery and execution; the repository must provide assertions, fixtures, application and database lifecycle, retries, reporting, visual baselines, and artifact policy.
project_and_compatibility.authoring_and_async_model: Tests use normal Go functions such as func TestName(t *testing.T), synchronous-looking Rod calls, contexts, goroutines, channels, and two-step event waits. Methods returning errors support explicit Go error handling; Must-prefixed methods panic by default and WithPanic can redirect failures to a test-aware handler that stops the current goroutine. There is no command queue, Gherkin layer, keyword DSL, or JavaScript async/await runtime.
project_and_compatibility.build_pipeline_coupling: Rod navigates to a URL and does not transform, instrument, or bundle frontend source. It can exercise the production Parcel build served by Gin or the Parcel development server and its existing API proxy. It does not require Vite, a Parcel plugin, injected test runtime, or alternate module settings. A Go TestMain or CI job must ensure that the selected frontend and backend topology is built and reachable first.
project_and_compatibility.testability_instrumentation_required: No Rod-specific production script, route, source transform, or relaxed content-security policy is required. Stable IDs and accessible HTML improve selectors but are optional. Reliable project tests still need deterministic data setup, the existing Yahoo Finance mock/configuration path, a non-API-only server that serves built frontend assets, readiness checks, and database cleanup. Those can remain test infrastructure rather than production browser instrumentation.

maintenance_health.latest_stable_release: v0.116.2, published July 12, 2024. It is the latest tagged non-prerelease observed on August 22, 2026; pkg.go.dev also identifies v0.116.2 as the latest module version. The module remains below semantic version 1.0.
maintenance_health.release_cadence: Release cadence has stopped. Rod published roughly monthly releases from August 2023 through July 2024, including seven releases from January through July 2024, but no tagged release followed during the next 25 months through observation. This is a material maintenance-health failure for a browser driver whose protocol and browser security baseline move frequently.
maintenance_health.repository_activity: The default branch was pushed on August 11, 2026, but the 2025-2026 commits inspected were sponsor or documentation edits. The newest observed merged code changes were in December 2024. Community pull requests continued to arrive, including dependency and memory-state fixes in 2026, while 29 pull requests remained open. Recent activity therefore demonstrates user demand but not active integration of browser-driver maintenance.
maintenance_health.issue_health: GitHub showed 181 open issues and 29 open pull requests on August 22, 2026. Issue 1238, opened June 6, 2026, explicitly asks whether the project is feature-complete or in maintenance mode; its four replies are community comments and no maintainer answer was present. Current reports include stale dependencies, a per-session state memory leak, iframe limitations, and launcher hangs, with related fixes still open. A complete response-time and closure-time distribution was not collected, so quantitative issue trend is [uncertain].
maintenance_health.roadmap_and_deprecation_risk: No formal deprecation notice was found, and the repository is not archived. However, no current roadmap or maintenance-mode statement was found, the maintainer did not answer the June 2026 maintenance question, stable releases stopped in 2024, and substantive merges also stopped in 2024. Whether the project will resume active releases or rely on a maintained fork is [uncertain]; practical de facto maintenance and abandonment risk is high.
maintenance_health.dependency_currency: The main module declares Go 1.21 and six direct github.com/ysmood dependencies; its workflows run primary tests on Go 1.22 and only compile on Go 1.18. The Open Asset Allocator module uses Go 1.26.5. Rod's default Chromium/CDP revision has not advanced with current browsers, and generated device profiles still contain Chrome 114 user agents. Compatibility with Go 1.26.5 and current installed Chrome was not executed, so current runtime compatibility is [uncertain].
maintenance_health.wrapper_upstream_lag: Rod is not a wrapper over WebDriver or Playwright, but it generates CDP types and pins a Chromium revision. Official compatibility documentation guarantees each Rod version only with its launcher.DefaultRevision. That revision and the latest release are from the 2024 maintenance period while users are now filing Chrome 150-related work. This creates roughly two years of browser/protocol integration lag; using a newer system Chrome may work but lies outside the documented guarantee.
maintenance_health.maintainer_concentration: Very high bus-factor risk. GitHub contributor data gives ysmood 715 commits, while the next observed contributor has 9 and the next four have 7 or 6. Recent sponsor/documentation commits are also from ysmood, while community code pull requests remain open. The contribution guide describes distributed governance in principle, but no organizational owner, funded maintenance team, published succession plan, or active multi-maintainer review distribution was evidenced.

community_adoption.npm_downloads: Not applicable. Rod has no official npm package and requires no Node runtime. The comparable registry signal is pkg.go.dev's 1,021 known importing Go modules, observed August 22, 2026.
community_adoption.github_metrics: Observed August 22, 2026: go-rod/rod had 7,067 stars, 479 forks, 181 open issues, 29 open pull requests, and a combined GitHub open_issues_count of 210. The default branch was last pushed August 11, 2026. The contributor API showed ysmood at 715 contributions and a steep drop to 9 for the next contributor, but an exact all-time contributor count and GitHub dependency-graph dependent count were not captured, so those submetrics are [uncertain].
community_adoption.ecosystem_usage: pkg.go.dev records 1,021 known importing modules. The maintainer's adoption discussion lists recognizable users including charmbracelet/vhs, Authelia, ProjectDiscovery Nuclei, Katana and httpx, Storj, Botkube, Sigstore, GoNB, and gowitness. Community comments include E2E testing with Testcontainers as well as scraping, screenshots, PDF generation, authentication, and automation. The evidence is meaningful for Go browser automation, but much usage is scraping or rendering rather than E2E test suites.
community_adoption.community_support: The project provides a docs site, Go API reference, examples, repository tests, FAQ, GitHub issues and discussions, and a Discord link. The documentation explains launch, selectors, network interception, emulation, debugging flags, and low-level CDP use. Troubleshooting often points users to source tests and issue search. Community questions continue, but current maintainer response is weak and the docs do not provide an integrated E2E harness guide comparable to complete test frameworks.
community_adoption.adoption_trend: Rod retains a sizable Go audience, with 7,067 stars, 1,021 known importers, and new use-case comments through late 2025. At the same time, release and merge activity declined sharply after 2024, and users discussed moving to a fork in 2026. No normalized historical series for stars, importers, or active E2E repositories was collected, so whether real adoption is stable or declining is [uncertain].
community_adoption.adoption_metric_normalization: There is no npm measurement. The 1,021 figure is pkg.go.dev's current count of known modules importing github.com/go-rod/rod; it includes direct and indexed public imports for scraping, PDF/screenshot generation, security tools, automation, and E2E testing, and does not count unique users, private modules, downloads, or active deployments. GitHub stars and forks are repository-wide lifetime vanity signals and do not isolate the Go testing composition evaluated here.

browser_and_runtime_coverage.browser_engines: Practical first-class coverage is Chromium through the Chrome DevTools Protocol. Rod can launch downloaded Chromium or discover installed Chrome and Microsoft Edge. It does not provide production-ready Firefox, WebKit, or native Safari projects. The official compatibility page says Firefox was supporting CDP and Safari had no plan to do so, but Rod gives no guaranteed Firefox target and current Firefox automation uses other protocols. This candidate therefore cannot provide a cross-engine Linux matrix.
browser_and_runtime_coverage.browser_protocol: Rod communicates directly with the browser's Chrome DevTools Protocol endpoint over WebSocket/JSON-RPC and exposes generated low-level proto calls beneath its high-level API. It does not use W3C WebDriver or WebDriver BiDi. Deep Chromium control enables network and emulation features but ties compatibility to Chrome's evolving CDP and Rod's pinned generated revision.
browser_and_runtime_coverage.headless_and_headed_modes: Headless is the launcher default and is suitable for CI. Headed mode is enabled with launcher.Headless(false), the -rod=show option, or equivalent defaults. The launcher supports the new Chromium headless switch and Xvfb on Linux; the official image installs Xvfb for headed execution. DevTools can be opened automatically in headed mode.
browser_and_runtime_coverage.browser_version_management: Rod searches for a local browser or downloads a statically selected Chromium snapshot to its cache. A specific revision or binary can be configured, and a remote launcher image can centralize the browser. This supports pinning, but only the default revision is guaranteed compatible with a Rod release. Since that default has not been released forward since 2024, teams must choose between an old guaranteed browser, an unguaranteed current system browser, or maintaining a fork and compatibility tests.
browser_and_runtime_coverage.parallel_browser_support: Rod operations are documented as thread-safe and it includes browser and page pools. Go goroutines and testing parallelism can run multiple pages, incognito contexts, or browser processes. There is no declarative browser-project matrix, selected-engine CLI, test shard planner, or merged result format; browser versions and job distribution are project-owned. Firefox/WebKit matrices are unavailable.
browser_and_runtime_coverage.mobile_emulation: Page.Emulate and predefined device descriptors set viewport, screen size, device scale factor, user agent, touch/mobile capability, and orientation. Additional CDP calls can set related metrics. The bundled profiles are dated, including many Chrome 114 user agents and old named devices, and represent Chromium desktop emulation rather than physical Android, iOS, Mobile Safari, or mobile Firefox.
browser_and_runtime_coverage.real_browser_fidelity: Rod can drive installed branded Chrome or Edge, which provides those real Chromium products, or a downloaded Chromium snapshot. Automation flags and headless rendering can still differ from an interactive user session. There is no WebKit result that can be mistaken for Safari: native Safari is simply unsupported. Device emulation does not turn Chromium into Mobile Safari or a physical device.
browser_and_runtime_coverage.environment_determinism_controls: High-level APIs cover viewport/device emulation, user agent, headers, cookies, network conditions, and browser launch environment such as TZ. Generated CDP proto calls can additionally control locale, timezone, geolocation, permissions, virtual time, media features, and device metrics where the pinned Chromium supports them. Rod provides no unified test fixture for clock, seeded randomness, animation suppression, fonts, or reduced motion; these require low-level calls, JavaScript/CSS injection, launch configuration, and repository conventions.

application_fit.dynamic_dom_synchronization: Rod's single-element queries poll until an element appears, actions can wait for visibility/interactability/stability, and Page.WaitDOMStable, WaitStable, WaitRequestIdle, WaitEvent, Race, and JavaScript conditions provide explicit synchronization. This can handle HTMX requests and Handlebars rendering without fixed sleeps. Unlike a locator abstraction, an Element is a concrete remote object and is not automatically reacquired after an HTMX replacement; tests must store selector intent and query again before later actions or assertions. Assertions from Go libraries are not automatically polled.
application_fit.routing_support: Direct navigation, current URL inspection, back/forward/reload, navigation history, and the v0.116.2 ResetNavigationHistory API cover normal browser routing. Navigo pushState changes may not emit a full page lifecycle event, so tests need a URL or route-specific DOM polling helper rather than relying only on WaitNavigation. Fresh incognito contexts or explicit route reset are needed between tests. Gin must continue serving the SPA shell for direct deep links.
application_fit.locator_model: Rod supports CSS, XPath, JavaScript, visible-text regular expressions, tree traversal, and search through nested frames and shadow DOM. A single-element query waits for a match, but it returns a concrete element, does not enforce strict uniqueness, and has no first-class getByRole, getByLabel, or test-id policy. Accessible locators can be encoded with CSS attributes or JavaScript helpers. Stable IDs and selector helper functions are important for reacquiring HTMX-replaced nodes.
application_fit.form_interaction: Element APIs cover focus, blur, click, input, keyboard typing, key actions, selection, file upload, color/time inputs, touch, and property inspection. These can exercise native focus/blur, validation, dynamic rows, hidden-value synchronization, and input event handling rather than mutating application state directly. Tests should use user actions for behavior and reserve Eval/Property for observing hidden values or validation state. Post-action waits and assertions remain custom.
application_fit.canvas_and_download_support: Rod can capture full-page or element screenshots and convert a canvas element directly to image bytes with CanvasToImage/MustCanvasToImage, enabling pixel or image decoding in Go. Browser.WaitDownload and MustWaitDownload register a two-step wait and return downloaded bytes, after which tests can inspect payload content. Rod does not manage visual baselines, masks, tolerances, review, or per-browser diffs; Chart.js semantic access, animation completion, and image comparison must be implemented by the project.
application_fit.network_and_api_access: Browser- or page-scoped HijackRequests can observe, continue, fail, or modify requests and responses; CDP events and WaitRequestIdle cover observation and synchronization. Go's net/http client can seed and reset REST fixtures in the same tests. Browser-originated Yahoo Finance traffic can be intercepted, but this application performs external integration server-side, so the existing Go Yahoo Finance mock and overridden backend configuration are the more reliable boundary. HAR replay and an integrated API fixture context are absent.
application_fit.same_origin_support: Rod controls a normal external browser and can navigate to either the consolidated Gin production origin or Parcel's development origin and API proxy. No CORS change is needed when the existing topology keeps browser traffic same-origin. If Rod or the browser runs in its remote Docker image, the base URL must use a network-reachable host or service name rather than localhost inside the browser container.
application_fit.test_isolation: Browser.Incognito creates an isolated browser context for cookies and storage, and a fresh browser per test is also possible. Go t.Cleanup can close pages and contexts. Database state remains outside browser isolation. This repository already has Testcontainers PostgreSQL/Flyway setup, initialized fixtures, Yahoo Finance mocking, and per-test SQL cleanup builders, which can be reused or factored for E2E tests; unsafe t.Parallel use must be prevented until each worker has independent data or a database.
application_fit.external_server_model: Rod naturally tests an independently started server: code passes a configured base URL to Browser.Page or Page.Navigate. Local Compose, a TestMain-started Gin server, Parcel port 8000, or a CI deployment are all possible. Rod has no baseURL fixture, port reservation, or server health manager, so environment parsing and readiness belong in the Go harness.
application_fit.application_lifecycle: Rod does not build Parcel, start Gin, run Docker Compose or Testcontainers, wait for Flyway, or tear down PostgreSQL. Standard Go TestMain, contexts, t.Cleanup, os/exec, net/http polling, and Testcontainers can supply those concerns. This is a relative advantage because the repository already runs PostgreSQL and Flyway through Testcontainers and starts an API-only Gin server in inttest, but E2E work must add built static assets or a Parcel server, browser lifecycle, HTTP readiness, and cancellation-safe cleanup.
application_fit.visual_regression_workflow: Core support stops at page, full-page, element, scroll, and canvas image capture. Baseline naming/storage, update approval, image diffing, masks, tolerances, font and animation stabilization, CI diff reports, and platform-specific baselines require a Go image library and custom harness. The official image includes common fonts, which can improve consistency. Chart.js tests should assert deterministic data and canvas readiness before a narrowly scoped image comparison.
application_fit.accessibility_audit_integration: Rod can inject and evaluate axe-core JavaScript or call Chromium's generated CDP Accessibility domain, so open-source audits are technically possible. There is no official axe integration, accessible locator API, ARIA snapshot assertion, violation formatter, or accessibility report pipeline. Script loading, rules, frame handling, result conversion, and artifact output are custom, and automated checks still require manual accessibility review.

reliability.waiting_model: Element lookup retries until presence, and Rod provides visibility, enabled, writable, interactable, stable, DOM-stable, page-stable, load, navigation, request-idle, repaint, event, and arbitrary JavaScript waits. Its two-step event APIs register before the triggering action to avoid missed events. Timeouts are context-derived and can be applied to browser, page, or element chains. There are no web-first assertion matchers, and retained Element objects are not locator-like, so postconditions and HTMX node reacquisition need explicit polling helpers.
reliability.flake_controls: Go testing supplies per-test deadlines through contexts and selective execution but has no built-in retries. Rod supplies configurable sleepers/backoff, chained timeouts, event waits, Race selectors, and deterministic explicit waits; the documentation discourages time.Sleep. Retry policy, repeat-until-failure scripts, first-attempt preservation, and failure classification must be added around go test. Browser/CDP version staleness is an additional flake and breakage risk that test-level retries cannot correct.
reliability.isolation_model: The preferred model is a fresh incognito context or browser per test plus t.Cleanup, with unique or restored PostgreSQL data. A browser can be shared at suite scope for speed while contexts isolate cookies and storage. Serial stateful scenarios can intentionally share a context, but ordinary tests should not. Go package-level TestMain and the repository's existing SQL cleanup facilities fit this model; browser isolation does not serialize or reset database state.
reliability.resource_usage: The test process is a Go binary and does not add a Node test runtime, but Chromium dominates CPU and memory. Fresh browser processes are heavier than pages or incognito contexts; pools can bound concurrency. Automatic downloads and the Ubuntu launcher image add browser, fonts, and system-library disk cost, while screenshots and CDP logs add artifacts. No Open Asset Allocator benchmark measured cold download size, peak memory, CPU, or suite duration, so quantitative resource use is [uncertain].
reliability.parallelism_controls: Rod is thread-safe and offers browser/page pools; Go testing exposes -parallel, package parallelism, t.Parallel, and test-name filters. Keeping database-mutating tests serial is simple by not calling t.Parallel and using one E2E package, while independent read-only scenarios can use bounded goroutines or tests. Cross-job shards, browser matrices, database allocation, and result merging are not Rod features and require GitHub Actions and harness conventions.
reliability.flake_observability: Go test -json exposes test start, output, pass, fail, skip, elapsed time, and rerun results, and custom wrappers can preserve a first failure before retry. Rod itself has no retry classification, quarantine registry, flaky-test status, historical database, or local trend dashboard. Repeat runs, attempt identifiers, JSON enrichment, and trend aggregation must be implemented or composed from open-source Go tooling.

diagnostics_and_developer_experience.failure_artifacts: Rod can produce page, full-page, scroll, element, and canvas screenshots; log CDP traffic; subscribe to console, exception, network, and lifecycle events; and save page/DOM data through APIs. Its own CI stores tmp/cdp-log artifacts. It does not automatically capture these on every test failure and has no integrated video, HAR, DOM/action trace archive, retention modes, or HTML artifact index. The test harness must register t.Cleanup and failure hooks and collect backend/container logs.
diagnostics_and_developer_experience.debugging_tools: Headed mode, automatic DevTools opening, slow motion, visual input trace overlays, CDP logging, and remote browser monitoring are built in. Normal Go breakpoints and IDE debugging apply because tests are Go. There is no test inspector, step runner, time-travel DOM viewer, watch UI, or pause-on-failure workflow comparable to an integrated browser test runner.
diagnostics_and_developer_experience.test_generation: Rod has no official browser recorder, scenario code generator, or accessible locator generator. Developers select CSS/text/XPath/JavaScript queries with browser DevTools and write Go code manually. Third-party generation would not remove the need to design HTMX waits, database fixtures, cleanup, and diagnostics.
diagnostics_and_developer_experience.reporters: The standard runner provides human-readable go test output and structured go test -json events. JUnit conversion, HTML reports, GitHub annotations, attachment indexing, retry metadata, and shard merging require third-party Go tools or custom code. Rod has no reporter API of its own, so browser artifacts must be linked to test names through harness conventions.
diagnostics_and_developer_experience.documentation_quality: The API reference is extensive and the docs site covers launch, selectors, network, emulation, debugging, examples, FAQ, and compatibility. Source tests provide many practical examples. Weaknesses are that documentation is not versioned as a rendered release site, some compatibility language is dated, device/browser references are old, E2E runner architecture is not covered, and current maintenance status is undocumented.
diagnostics_and_developer_experience.local_workflow: Developers can run one test with go test -run, run a package, use standard IDE test actions, switch to headed mode with -rod=show, add devtools/slow/trace flags, and debug with Go breakpoints. Browser downloads are automatic and cacheable. Re-running only failures, watching files, interactively selecting scenarios, and opening a unified report require scripts or IDE facilities rather than Rod.
diagnostics_and_developer_experience.failure_log_correlation: Rod loggers and event handlers can timestamp CDP, browser console, exception, and network events, while Go tests can include test names and UTC timestamps. The existing integration infrastructure already fans PostgreSQL logs into testing.TB and prints Flyway logs. Correlating those with Gin, Parcel, browser, and screenshot artifacts still requires a shared run/test ID, synchronized timestamps, bounded log capture, and custom attachment naming; Rod does not correlate processes automatically.
diagnostics_and_developer_experience.artifact_data_exposure: Screenshots, DOM/page content, download bytes, request and response bodies, headers, cookies, console output, CDP logs, and browser user-data directories can expose portfolio records, credentials, and Yahoo responses. Rod provides selective event handling but no artifact redaction pipeline. Use synthetic fixtures and incognito profiles, avoid persistent user data, filter headers/bodies before writing, restrict artifact access and retention, and do not upload raw CDP traffic by default.

github_actions_fit.official_ci_support: Rod maintains example workflows that run Go tests on ubuntu-latest and upload CDP logs, plus macOS and Windows jobs. It publishes an Ubuntu-based remote launcher image. There is no Rod-specific GitHub Action or application-test workflow template; a normal job uses setup-go, builds Parcel, starts Testcontainers or Compose, runs go test, and uploads custom artifacts.
github_actions_fit.browser_caching: Cache the Go module/build caches and $HOME/.cache/rod/browser using keys that include OS, architecture, Rod version, and Chromium revision, or pull a pinned remote launcher image. Caching avoids each cold runner downloading Chromium. Because the official image tag and upstream Dockerfile bases are not digest-pinned, production CI should pin an image digest and explicitly control upgrades rather than rely on latest mutable state.
github_actions_fit.artifact_integration: Screenshots, go test JSON/JUnit conversions, CDP logs, downloads, and Compose service logs are ordinary files and can be uploaded with actions/upload-artifact under an always condition. Rod does not create a report directory or attachment manifest, so failure hooks, naming, secret filtering, retention, and links between tests and files are custom. Integration effort is moderate to high.
github_actions_fit.sharding_and_matrix_support: GitHub Actions can matrix over shard indexes, configurations, or installed Chromium channels, and go test can select package/test subsets. Rod has no native shard calculation, blob report, report merger, or declarative browser project. A deterministic test manifest and JUnit/JSON merge step are required. Shared PostgreSQL tests should remain in one serial job until each shard receives an independent database and fixture namespace.
github_actions_fit.container_compatibility: A host-run Go test can control a host-installed/downloaded browser while the application uses Docker Compose or Testcontainers, which avoids nested container complexity. Alternatively, ghcr.io/go-rod/rod exposes a remote launcher on port 7317 and can join the application network. The harness must configure reachable hostnames, ports, shared networks, health checks, shm/resources, and a pinned image; localhost inside the browser container is not the runner host.
github_actions_fit.failure_cleanup: Browser.Close, page/context cleanup, launcher.Cleanup, and t.Cleanup handle orderly exits; launcher leakless mode is designed to kill browser processes if the Go process crashes. TestMain can stop Gin and terminate Testcontainers as the existing integration suite does. GitHub Actions must still collect logs and run Compose down with volume/orphan cleanup under always, because cancellation or runner termination can bypass Go cleanup and leak external resources.

cost_and_risk.open_source_completeness: Rod, Go testing, Testcontainers, image comparison libraries, axe-core injection, and common JUnit/HTML converters can provide a fully local open-source stack. No paid service is required. However, Rod alone is not feature-complete as an E2E framework: reporters, retries, visual baselines, accessibility integration, videos/traces, lifecycle, and flake analytics must be composed or built, and Firefox/WebKit coverage cannot be added through Rod.
cost_and_risk.optional_cloud_dependency: No cloud is required for authoring, Chromium execution, screenshots, downloads, request interception, or CI. A remote browser service, visual review platform, or analytics dashboard is optional. Cloud services could add current browsers or managed artifacts, but they do not repair Rod's stale generated CDP API, and native Safari or Firefox would require a different driver rather than merely a Rod dashboard.
cost_and_risk.migration_cost: Tests bind to Go, Rod's Must/error APIs, concrete Element handles, CDP-specific events/proto types, and custom lifecycle/reporting helpers. Scenario intent, REST fixtures, Testcontainers code, and database cleanup can survive a migration, but browser interactions, waits, locators, interception, emulation, and artifacts would need rewriting for Playwright, WebDriver, or Cypress. Low-level proto usage increases lock-in.
cost_and_risk.security_and_supply_chain: The Go module is MIT-licensed and has a relatively small direct dependency set, but all six direct dependencies are under the primary maintainer's ysmood namespace. The August 17, 2026 OpenSSF Scorecard was 3.5/10: no security policy, SAST, fuzzing, signed releases, pinned workflow/container dependencies, or least-privilege workflow tokens were detected. Browser setup downloads executable archives from external hosts; the guaranteed default browser is old, creating browser-vulnerability risk. Pin Go sums and image digests, scan dependencies/images, control egress, sandbox Chromium, and avoid an obsolete browser baseline.
cost_and_risk.custom_harness_burden: High, though lower than a new Go stack because this repository already has TestMain, Testcontainers PostgreSQL/Flyway, Yahoo Finance mocking, SQL cleanup, and log fan-out. New work still includes a non-API-only application server or Parcel lifecycle, base URL/readiness, browser/context fixtures, selector and polling helpers for HTMX/Navigo, assertion strategy, retries/repeats, screenshots and browser events on failure, JUnit/HTML output, visual baselines, accessibility audits, shard/database policy, artifact redaction, and cancellation-safe cleanup.
cost_and_risk.capability_delivery_tier: Core Rod: Chromium CDP control, launcher/download, headless/headed modes, contexts, pages, selectors, explicit waits, input, navigation, network interception, emulation, screenshots, canvas bytes, downloads, debugging trace/monitoring, and pools. Standard Go/testing: discovery, subtests, cleanup, filters, JSON events, parallel controls, HTTP fixture clients, and assertions selected by the project. Existing repository infrastructure: PostgreSQL/Flyway Testcontainers, Yahoo mock, fixture state, cleanup SQL, and database logs. Community/custom: JUnit/HTML reporting, retries, visual regression, axe integration, lifecycle/readiness, log correlation, redaction, sharding, and flake trends. Paid cloud: none required. Unavailable in this stack: first-class Firefox, WebKit, and Safari execution.
cost_and_risk.ai_execution_boundary: Rod and Go testing are deterministic conventional software and require no LLM, AI credentials, model egress, or per-test inference cost. Any optional AI-assisted authoring can remain outside CI and produce reviewed Go tests. Browser execution, assertions, fixture setup, and failure reporting retain a complete non-AI path.

evidence_and_decision.confidence: High confidence in release age, repository activity, license, stars/forks/issues, registry importers, protocol/browser limits, documented APIs, and local repository integration architecture because these come from first-party source, APIs, and local files. Medium confidence in ecosystem breadth, issue trend, future maintenance, and the weighted fit score because adoption metrics are broad proxies and maintainers have not stated project status. Low confidence in current Chrome/Go runtime behavior and application-specific flake/resource performance until a spike is executed.
evidence_and_decision.hard_gate_result: FAIL overall for primary selection. PASS: open-source Go authoring, Linux/GitHub Ubuntu x64, black-box Parcel/Gin operation, Chromium headless/headed execution, HTMX-capable explicit waits, Navigo history primitives, realistic forms, canvas/download APIs, network interception, external server access, and reuse of existing Go Testcontainers fixtures. CONDITIONAL: robust DOM replacement, retries, reports, visual testing, accessibility, diagnostics, and database-safe parallelism require custom code. FAIL: actively maintained/current browser baseline, current guaranteed CDP compatibility, and first-class Firefox/WebKit/Safari coverage. The defined empirical project spike is also not complete, but the maintenance and engine failures are independently sufficient for exclusion.
evidence_and_decision.deal_breakers: The latest release is more than two years old, substantive merges stopped in 2024, and the only documented browser compatibility guarantee is tied to an old pinned Chromium/CDP revision. Rod is effectively Chromium-only and cannot supply Firefox, WebKit, or native Safari coverage. It also lacks an integrated runner-level retry, reporter, trace/video, visual-regression, accessibility, and shard workflow. These are exclusion-level risks for selecting the best-maintained primary E2E tool, even though Go integration and Chromium automation are technically viable.
evidence_and_decision.project_fit_score: 55.6/100 provisional [uncertain]. Weighted calculation: application fit 70/100 x 30% = 21.00; maintenance 25/100 x 20% = 5.00; reliability 62/100 x 15% = 9.30; adoption 65/100 x 15% = 9.75; CI experience 55/100 x 10% = 5.50; diagnostics 48/100 x 5% = 2.40; cost and risk 52/100 x 5% = 2.60; total 55.55, rounded to 55.6. Existing Go integration infrastructure raises application fit, but stale maintenance, one-engine coverage, and custom harness obligations dominate. No runtime spike or resource benchmark was performed.
evidence_and_decision.recommendation: Excluded as the primary E2E choice. Rod is a credible Go-native Chromium automation library and could reuse this repository's Testcontainers, Yahoo mock, SQL cleanup, and testing conventions, but its July 2024 final release, old guaranteed CDP/browser baseline, concentrated maintenance, open dependency work, Chromium-only scope, and missing integrated diagnostics/reporting make it inconsistent with the research goal of a best-maintained and broadly community-adopted E2E tool. Retain it only as a Go-specific comparison or for a narrowly Chromium-only internal harness if the project accepts owning a maintained fork.
evidence_and_decision.empirical_project_spike_result: Not performed [uncertain]. No Rod dependency, browser binary, E2E package, or CI workflow was added or executed. A proof would still need to cover HTMX replacement with element reacquisition; Navigo deep links and back/forward cleanup; focus, blur, native validation, hidden values, and dynamic rows; deterministic Chart.js canvas bytes and screenshot diff; download payload verification; REST fixtures and the existing Yahoo mock; disposable PostgreSQL cleanup under failure; current Go 1.26.5 and current Chrome compatibility; and a forced failure that captures secret-safe screenshots, console/network/CDP evidence, Gin/Flyway/PostgreSQL logs, and guaranteed browser/container teardown.
